passages.t: The lesson learned: Levites, consecration, and song
passages.happening:
David builds himself houses in the City of David, prepares a place for the ark, and pitches a tent for it (verse 1). Then he says, “No one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, because the LORD has chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister before Him forever” (verse 2). He gathers all Israel and the priests and Levites, clan by clan (verses 3-11).

He tells the Levite leaders to consecrate themselves (verse 12). “It was because you Levites were not with us the first time that the LORD our God burst forth in anger against us. For we did not consult Him about the proper order” (verse 13). ‘So the priests and Levites consecrated themselves’ (verse 14), ‘And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded’ (verse 15). David has the Levites appoint singers ‘to lift up their voices with joy’ (verse 16): Heman, Asaph and Ethan with cymbals, others with harps and lyres, Chenaniah to direct the music, gatekeepers, and priests with trumpets (verses 17-24).
passages.hearers:
Three months earlier the first attempt ended in Uzzah's death. Chapter 14 showed God still establishing David. This chapter is about the difference between the two attempts. The first time the ark rode on a new cart, as the Philistines had once sent it back, and no one asked what the law said. This time the ark goes up on Levite shoulders, the priests are consecrated, and the procession is ordered around worship.

The ark was fitted with poles so it could be carried without being touched, and the law gave the carrying of the holy things to the Kohathite Levites, on their shoulders. The Levites were the tribe set apart for the sanctuary; the priests were the branch of Levi descended from Aaron.

David's words in verse 13 name the lesson. The word for the proper order, mishpat, usually means justice; here it means the right way of doing things. The problem was the absence of darash, seeking God, the very word on which Saul was judged. To consecrate, qadash, was to set oneself apart for holy work, with washing and ritual purity.

The lists are not filler. They show that worship was now being done in the right order. The terms Alamoth and Sheminith in verses 20 and 21 also appear in psalm titles, and their meaning is uncertain.
passages.later: The law said of the Kohathites, ‘they were to carry on their shoulders the holy objects for which they were responsible’ (Numbers 7:9).
passages.hard:
Was God unfair to strike Uzzah, and does this chapter blame Uzzah or David?

Uzzah's death strikes many readers as harsh: he reached out to steady the ark, apparently with good motives. This chapter gives David's own verdict in verse 13. The fault lay with the whole leadership, David included, for ignoring the law's clear instructions about who should carry the ark and how. Some interpreters stress that the holy things were plainly guarded by the death penalty, so the danger was known, not arbitrary. Others stress that the story teaches the seriousness of God's presence at a founding moment, much as the deaths of Aaron's sons did when the tabernacle began. The difficulty does not vanish. But the chapter shows a king who takes responsibility rather than blaming God or Uzzah, and who comes back with reverence instead of giving up.
passages.asks: David admitted that they had not consulted God about the proper order. Ask where your zeal has run ahead of asking God. And ask what it would look like to take responsibility for a failure rather than blame someone else.

passages.t: The ark comes up, and Michal at the window
passages.happening:
‘So David, the elders of Israel, and the commanders of thousands went with rejoicing to bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the house of Obed-edom’ (verse 25). ‘And because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark’ (verse 26), they sacrifice seven bulls and seven rams. David wears a robe of fine linen and a linen ephod (verse 27). ‘So all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting’ (verse 28), with rams' horns, trumpets, cymbals, harps and lyres.

‘As the ark of the covenant of the LORD was entering the City of David, Saul’s daughter Michal looked down from a window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart’ (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
By bringing the ark to Jerusalem, David made his new capital the religious center of all the tribes. The tabernacle itself stood at Gibeon. The Chronicler's interest is in what it meant for worship. His first readers, after the exile, had a rebuilt temple and working orders of Levites but no king; these lists gave them roots in David's own ordering of worship.

Chronicles pairs careful order with exuberant joy, simchah. Obedience is not presented as joyless. The linen ephod was a priestly garment, and David's wearing it shows the king taking part in worship, not claiming to be a priest.

The chapter closes with one verse about Michal, taken from 2 Samuel 6:16. The Chronicler leaves out the longer quarrel between David and Michal in 2 Samuel, but the single glance from the window is enough. In the middle of joy there is contempt, and it comes from the house of Saul, whose failure to seek God began the story of David.
passages.later: Second Samuel says that David ‘danced with all his might before the LORD’ (2 Samuel 6:14). A psalm says, ‘Serve the LORD with gladness; come into His presence with joyful songs’ (Psalm 100:2).
passages.asks: David danced, and Michal despised him in her heart. Ask whether you are more at home with order or with joy in worship, and what you might learn from the other. And ask whom you have looked down on for worshiping in a way that embarrassed you.
